candidates.title: Reading between the pixels: what image overlays cost brands and how we detect them at catalog scale
candidates.summary: How we reuse stored image embeddings to screen product photos so a vision-language model reviews less than one in ten Retailers shopping on Faire scroll past dozens of product images on a single page and make split-second decisions about which listings deserve a closer look. For the independent brands selling on Faire, that image is often the first sales pitch. Many of those images were first made for a different context, like a brand’s Instagram, its own storefront, or a mockup template, and they arrive with text and graphics added on top. The most common types of such overlays are stock watermarks, social handles, website addresses, promotional text, and brand logos. The most common types of overlays. All examples pictured in this article are mock listings. Faire’s image guidelines require brands not to include any words, watermarks, or logos on the featured product image, because overlays can take attention away from the product itself: they can cover part of it, make claims that may be misleading, or simply make the photo look cluttered. We set this guideline based on marketplace design principles, but we wanted to dig deeper into the problem, understand its real cost, and find better solutions. To do that, we first had to identify overlays correctly and efficiently. candidates.title: De-identifying text at scale: How Airbnb protects personal data in AI training
candidates.summary: Here’s how Airbnb detects and replaces personal data in messages, reviews, and support chats before it reaches a model. By: Emelin Flores , Alex Klimov , Lee Formyduval , Bahador Nooraei Introduction Airbnb is built on trust. Every night that a guest books a stay, or a host welcomes someone into their home, that trust is backed by information they’ve shared with us, which includes personally identifiable information (PII) such as names, home location, current location, and payment details. We now use transaction information to train machine learning models. Before we do so, we remove PII to minimize the number of copies of this information and prevent leakage into and through our models. As we’ve written before , Airbnb maintains a shared taxonomy as to what constitutes PII, from commonly used fields such as names and card numbers to less frequently used fields such as precise location coordinates. We use de-identification to remove PII and replace it with simulated data that’s as realistic as possible to maximize its usefulness for ML model training. Decisions relating to user privacy start as policy. These policies are set and maintained by Airbnb’s Privacy Architecture team, with engagement from Legal, Policy, and Engineering. Engineering then implements policy decisions as code. This post focuses on text de-identification.
